domain_assessment.domain: Building and fire-code plan review for a performance-based smoke-control design in an adaptive-reuse high-rise project
domain_assessment.role: Municipal plan-review official in a building and fire division responsible for permitting and life-safety sign-off
domain_assessment.objective: Complete the statutory plan review within 30 days while ensuring that the non-prescriptive atrium smoke-control design, commissioning process, inspections, and occupancy decision adequately protect life safety
domain_assessment.incident_type: High-rise adaptive-reuse permitting case involving a performance-based atrium smoke-control design, construction fire-door deficiencies, a temporary occupancy request before system integration testing, and a later unrelated trash-chute fire

decision_points.summary: Approve the performance-based CFD smoke-control design after seeking a targeted written clarification about the stack-effect assumption rather than requiring a full external peer review.
evidence_before: CFD-based smoke-control report
Halkirk & Vance's experience with prior atrium designs
A neighboring jurisdiction's approval of a similar design
The participant's review of the assumptions
A statutory 30-day review period
Limited staffing and no budget for outside peer review
evidence_after: The engineering firm provided additional written documentation about the stack-effect assumption
The participant approved the design after that exchange
A later trash-chute fire was determined to be unrelated to the atrium system
goals_constraints: Ensure the design performs as the code intends during a fire
Avoid a roughly three-week delay associated with a full peer review
Work within staffing and peer-review budget constraints
alternatives: Approve the submitted package without further scrutiny
Request a targeted clarification on the consequential stack-effect assumption
Require a full independent external peer review
decision_points.decision_basis: The participant treated firm reputation and neighboring approval as relevant but insufficient, identified a building-specific uncertainty in the stack-effect treatment, and obtained written clarification on that assumption before approval.
decision_points.time_pressure: Moderate to high: a 30-day statutory review clock, staffing shortages, city pressure to advance housing, and an estimated three-week external-review delay.
decision_points.uncertainty: Moderate: the design was performance based and non-prescriptive, but uncertainty was narrowed by focusing on the assumption judged most consequential for egress.

decision_points.summary: Select the newer risk-informed commissioning protocol and add auditable interim checkpoints and documentation standards to manage its qualitatively defined thresholds.
evidence_before: Option A was better matched to the atrium geometry under applicable guidance
Option A's thresholds were partly qualitative
Option B offered binary pass-fail criteria
Option B was less sensitive to relevant atrium failure modes
evidence_after: Defined interim checkpoints and documentation standards were incorporated into the selected protocol
The protocol became intended to be both technically appropriate and administratively defensible
goals_constraints: Choose a technically appropriate test for the actual atrium geometry
Maintain auditable and defensible enforcement criteria
Avoid substituting administrative simplicity for technical fit
alternatives: Use Option A, the newer risk-informed test with partly qualitative thresholds
Use Option B, the older prescriptive binary smoke test
decision_points.decision_basis: The participant selected the technically better-fitting protocol while modifying its documentation and checkpoint structure to address enforceability.
decision_points.time_pressure: Not explicitly quantified at this decision point; project construction and commissioning progression create an implicit operational schedule.
decision_points.uncertainty: Moderate: Option A had qualitatively specified thresholds, but the participant operationalized those thresholds rather than avoiding the option.

decision_points.summary: Maintain the original building-wide random-sample fire-door inspection plan after three deficiencies appeared on floors 8, 11, and 14.
evidence_before: Three fire-door deficiencies on floors 8, 11, and 14
Approximately 150 doors had been checked
Crews rotated randomly across the building
The observed count was described as within ordinary project-size variation
evidence_after: A building-wide random sample produced a defect rate consistent with the initial findings
No evidence showed that the three identified floors were worse than the remainder of the building
goals_constraints: Detect whether a localized construction-quality problem existed
Avoid overconcentrating inspection resources based on a potentially random early pattern
alternatives: Concentrate inspections on floors 8, 11, and 14 based on the apparent pattern
Continue the original random-sample inspection plan across all floors
decision_points.decision_basis: Although the participant initially considered a crew-specific explanation, they considered random crew allocation, denominator information, and ordinary variation, then retained the representative sampling plan.
decision_points.time_pressure: Not explicitly stated; construction was underway and inspection timing was operationally relevant.
decision_points.uncertainty: Initially moderate, then reduced after the broader sample showed no localized elevation in defect rates.

decision_points.summary: Grant temporary occupancy only for floors not dependent on the untested atrium system, withholding the remaining floors until full integration testing passed.
evidence_before: The developer faced a financing deadline
Full alarm and smoke-system integration testing was approximately three weeks away
The contractor had a positive record on other city projects
A colleague cited a nearby building that received early partial occupancy without incident
Five-year city data showed an approximately 15 percent rework rate for comparable atrium integration tests
The untested system was the exact system on which the withheld floors depended
evidence_after: Temporary occupancy was limited to floors independent of the untested system
The atrium-dependent floors remained withheld pending a completed and passed integration test
The later trash-chute fire occurred after the occupancy decision and was unrelated to the atrium system
goals_constraints: Protect occupants from an unverified life-safety system
Respond proportionately to the developer's financing and schedule pressure
Avoid allowing general contractor reputation or anecdotal precedent to substitute for system-specific test evidence
alternatives: Grant broader early occupancy based on contractor history and nearby precedent
Grant limited occupancy only where floors did not depend on the untested atrium system
decision_points.decision_basis: The participant weighted system-specific historical rework data and the absence of completed integration testing more heavily than favorable but less diagnostic reputation and anecdotal precedent evidence.
decision_points.time_pressure: High: developer financing deadline and a three-week interval before full integration testing.
decision_points.uncertainty: High consequence but bounded: the untested system had a specific historical rework rate, and the participant used a conditional occupancy boundary to manage the uncertainty.

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “My first instinct was to wonder if we had a specific crew problem. But crews were rotated randomly across the building, and it was three deficiencies out of roughly 150 doors checked at that point—which is within the range you'd expect from ordinary variation on a project this size. So I kept the original random-sample inspection plan across all floors rather than concentrating just on those three.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Third-decision exchange concerning fire-door deficiencies, followed by the participant's report of the wider inspection sample.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: No clustering illusion is supported. The text briefly surfaces a possible localized-pattern hypothesis but explicitly evaluates it against random crew allocation, denominator information, expected variation, and a broader random sample. The participant does not infer a meaningful non-random cluster from the observed locations or alter the inspection plan on that basis.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The initial thought about a crew problem is a reasonable hypothesis-generation step after defects are found. It is promptly tested rather than treated as evidence of a pattern.
target_occurrence_audit.additional_evidence_needed: For a supported bias instance, the text would need to show the participant treating the three-floor pattern as meaningful despite the random allocation and insufficient sample, and acting on that inference. Such evidence must not be added in this zero-bias control.

revision.current_defect: None for the vocabulary-control requirement. The potential clustering cue is explicitly neutralized through appropriate denominator, randomization, and follow-up-sampling reasoning.
revision.minimal_change_instruction: Retain the current corrective reasoning and the building-wide sample result.
preserve: The three observed deficiencies on floors 8, 11, and 14
The decision to continue representative random sampling
avoid_creating: Any language that presents the floor locations alone as proof of a crew-specific or floor-specific problem
A decision to redirect inspections solely because the defects appear spatially grouped

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “Our own five-year data show something like a 15 percent rework rate on these atrium integration tests citywide, and that number is specific to the exact system we hadn't tested yet. So I granted occupancy only for the floors that didn't depend on the untested atrium system, and held back the rest until testing was done.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Fourth-decision temporary-occupancy exchange and the follow-up counterfactual probe.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: No probability neglect or base-rate neglect is supported. The participant explicitly retrieves and gives controlling weight to a system-specific five-year rework rate rather than relying on the contractor's general favorable history or a single nearby anecdote.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The conditional occupancy decision is proportionate risk management under an untested life-safety system, not a failure to consider likelihood information.
target_occurrence_audit.additional_evidence_needed: A supported instance would require evidence that the participant ignored, discounted, or failed to retrieve the relevant rework-rate information because of a vivid anecdote, reputation, or other non-diagnostic cue. No such addition is appropriate for this control.

revision.current_defect: None for the zero-occurrence control. The participant explicitly uses the relevant base-rate-like information and distinguishes it from non-specific positive evidence.
revision.minimal_change_instruction: Retain the 15 percent system-specific rework-rate reasoning and the requirement for a passed integration test for atrium-dependent floors.
avoid_creating: Language that discounts the rework rate as irrelevant because no incident occurred elsewhere
Language that grants atrium-dependent occupancy solely on reputation, precedent, urgency, or financing pressure

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “The occupancy call had the most riding on it, which is part of why I drew the line where I did rather than treating the contractor's general history as settling the question.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Uncertainty-reflection exchange following the temporary-occupancy decision.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: No optimism bias is supported. The participant does not express an unrealistically favorable expectation about completion, system performance, or the absence of rework. Instead, they constrain occupancy because the relevant integration test remains incomplete and has a documented rework history.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: Acknowledging schedule pressure and allowing limited occupancy for independent floors is a bounded operational accommodation, not evidence of an overly favorable forecast.
target_occurrence_audit.additional_evidence_needed: A supported instance would require a comparative overestimate of a favorable outcome, such as treating this project as materially less likely than comparable projects to require rework without evidence. That evidence is absent and should remain absent in the control.

revision.location: Decision point 4 and the later uncertainty reflection.
revision.current_defect: None for the control condition. The decision uses a conservative condition tied to passed testing rather than a favorable unsupported forecast.
revision.minimal_change_instruction: Keep the explicit distinction between the contractor's broad record and the untested system's specific evidence.
avoid_creating: Unqualified claims that the system will probably work because the contractor is reliable
Assurances that schedule pressure will not produce rework without supporting evidence

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “Option A was a newer risk-informed test, better matched to this atrium's geometry according to the guidance, but its thresholds were only partly and qualitatively defined.” “I built in defined interim checkpoints and documentation standards so the qualitative thresholds would still be auditable.”
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: No ambiguity effect is supported. Although Option A contains ambiguity in the form of qualitative thresholds, the participant does not avoid it merely because it is less precisely specified. They select the technically better-fitting option and reduce implementation ambiguity through auditability controls.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The added checkpoints and documentation standards are an appropriate governance response to qualitative criteria, not aversion-driven substitution of a known but less appropriate option.
target_occurrence_audit.additional_evidence_needed: A supported instance would require the participant to reject Option A principally because its outcomes or enforcement thresholds are less determinate, despite accepting that it is the better technical fit. That mechanism is not present and must not be inserted into this control.

revision.current_defect: None for the zero-bias control. The narrative shows ambiguity being managed rather than avoided.
revision.minimal_change_instruction: Retain the choice of Option A, the technical-fit rationale, and the specific auditability safeguards.
preserve: The contrast between qualitative and binary thresholds
Option B's lower sensitivity to relevant failure modes
Defined interim checkpoints and documentation standards
avoid_creating: A statement that selects Option B simply because binary criteria feel safer or easier to defend
A reframing in which qualitative thresholds alone determine the decision

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “The firm's documentation carried real weight, and so did the neighboring jurisdiction's approval.” “But I still went through the assumptions myself, and the stack-effect piece wasn't fully addressed for our specific geometry. I asked for a written clarification on that point specifically rather than taking the package at face value.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: First-decision approval exchange and the final advice to a newer reviewer.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: No authority bias is supported. The participant considers relevant credibility and prior external scrutiny but does not defer to either the engineering firm's status or another jurisdiction's approval as dispositive. They independently inspect a consequential assumption and seek building-specific evidence.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: A specialist firm's record and comparable jurisdictional approval are relevant evidence in a technical review, especially when they are used as contextual support rather than a substitute for analysis.
target_occurrence_audit.additional_evidence_needed: A supported authority-bias instance would require evidence that the participant accepted the design because a prestigious firm or approving authority endorsed it, while bypassing a material building-specific concern. The interview contains the contrary evidence and should continue to do so.

revision.current_defect: None for the control condition. Potential authority cues are clearly counterbalanced by independent assumption review and a targeted evidence request.
revision.minimal_change_instruction: Retain the distinction between giving reputation evidentiary weight and treating it as sufficient for approval.
preserve: The constrained alternative of a full peer review
avoid_creating: Language that makes prior approval or firm prestige the sole reason for approval
Removal of the participant's independent assessment of the stack-effect assumption

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “It held up fine, as it turned out—the fire was in the chute enclosure, unrelated to the atrium system.” “I wouldn't say the fire proved anything either way about that decision.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Post-incident reflection on the original design approval.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: No hindsight bias is supported. The participant separates the later outcome from the earlier decision, identifies the incident as causally unrelated to the atrium design, and explicitly rejects treating the fire as proof of whether the approval was correct.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The statement that the earlier clarification was worth pursuing is a retrospective assessment of a contemporaneously identified and documented concern, not a claim that the later event made the outcome foreseeable.
target_occurrence_audit.additional_evidence_needed: A supported instance would require the participant to claim that the later fire made the approval's correctness or the need for clarification obvious or predictable at the time, without separating causal relevance. That evidence is absent and would contaminate this control.

revision.current_defect: None for the zero-occurrence control. The participant includes an explicit causal-separation safeguard.
revision.minimal_change_instruction: Retain the statement that the trash-chute fire was unrelated to the atrium system and did not prove the original decision correct or incorrect.
preserve: The occurrence of the trash-chute fire after the occupancy decision
The determination that the fire was unrelated to the atrium system
avoid_creating: Claims that the later fire made the earlier concern obvious in advance
Outcome-based assertions that the approval was necessarily correct because no atrium failure occurred

additional_candidate_biases.supporting_quote: “My first instinct was to wonder if we had a specific crew problem.”
additional_candidate_biases.mechanism: The initial crew explanation could superficially resemble early anchoring on the first available causal hypothesis.
additional_candidate_biases.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The participant does not retain the initial hypothesis as an anchor, does not direct action from it, and explicitly tests it against random rotation, expected variation, and broader sampling before deciding.

additional_candidate_biases.supporting_quote: “It held up fine, as it turned out.”
additional_candidate_biases.mechanism: An isolated reading of this phrase could suggest evaluating the original approval through the subsequent outcome.
additional_candidate_biases.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The surrounding response expressly states that the later fire was unrelated to the atrium system and did not prove anything about the original approval. That explicit causal separation defeats an outcome-bias classification.

additional_candidate_biases.supporting_quote: “A colleague mentioned a nearby building that had gotten early partial occupancy without incident.”
additional_candidate_biases.mechanism: A salient nearby anecdote is introduced as potentially decision-relevant information.
additional_candidate_biases.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The participant does not allow the anecdote to drive the decision; they instead privilege relevant system-specific historical rework data and completed-test status.

nonbias_cues.cue: Consideration of Halkirk & Vance's experience and a neighboring jurisdiction's approval
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: These are relevant credibility and precedent signals, but the participant independently scrutinizes a building-specific assumption and requests written clarification. The authority information is not treated as dispositive.

nonbias_cues.cue: Selection of a protocol with qualitative thresholds
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: The participant does not avoid uncertainty or choose the more familiar binary option merely for certainty. They choose the better technical fit and implement concrete safeguards for auditability.

nonbias_cues.cue: Initial concern that defects on three floors could reflect a crew problem
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: An initial hypothesis is not itself a bias occurrence. The participant tests it with random allocation, the observed denominator, ordinary-variation reasoning, and broader sampling before maintaining the original plan.

nonbias_cues.cue: Developer financing deadline and pressure to keep housing moving
nonbias_cues.location: Opening objective statement and decision point 4.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: These are organizational and schedule constraints. The participant's limited occupancy decision maintains a system-dependent safety boundary rather than demonstrating distorted probability judgment or unwarranted optimism.

nonbias_cues.cue: The later trash-chute fire and statement that the original approval 'held up fine'
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: The participant identifies the fire as unrelated to the atrium system and expressly declines to regard it as proof about the earlier decision, preventing hindsight or outcome-based inference.

nonbias_cues.cue: Use of a targeted clarification rather than a full external peer review
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: This is a bounded, evidence-focused response to a particular material uncertainty under real time and budget constraints. The interview provides no evidence that the participant ignored additional known high-consequence deficiencies.

causal_claims.claim: The stack-effect assumption mattered for egress in the specific atrium geometry, so clarification was requested before approval.
causal_claims.assessment: Causally coherent as a decision-relevant engineering concern. The interview does not claim that the clarification alone caused safety, only that it resolved a review concern.

causal_claims.claim: The three observed door deficiencies did not establish a localized crew or floor problem.
causal_claims.assessment: Supported by the stated random crew rotation, the 150-door denominator, and the subsequent building-wide sample showing a consistent defect rate.

causal_claims.claim: Untested atrium integration systems carry a material possibility of rework, so atrium-dependent occupancy should await a passed integration test.
causal_claims.assessment: The decision logic is coherent because the cited rework rate is described as specific to the relevant untested system. The text uses the rate for risk management, not as proof that this project would fail.

causal_claims.claim: The later trash-chute fire does not establish the adequacy or inadequacy of the atrium smoke-control approval.
causal_claims.assessment: Strongly supported within the interview because the participant identifies the chute enclosure as the incident location and expressly states the issue was separate from the atrium system.

correlation_causation_risks.risk: The phrase 'it reinforced that the clarification I'd asked for ... was worth pursuing' could be read as retroactively linking the unrelated trash-chute fire to the earlier atrium-design concern.
correlation_causation_risks.mitigation_present: The same response says the fire was unrelated to the atrium system and did not prove anything either way about the original decision.

correlation_causation_risks.risk: A neighboring jurisdiction's prior approval could be mistaken for evidence that the present building will perform safely.
correlation_causation_risks.mitigation_present: The participant expressly treats the present building's geometry and stack-effect assumption as requiring separate review.

causal_audit.changed_variable: Not applicable. The hidden specification identifies engineering-firm reputation only as a paired-scenario counterfactual variable, while this interview is designated vocabulary_control and introduces no altered causal variable.
held_constant: Statutory review timeline and staffing constraints
Four decision points and their topical sequence
causal_audit.explanation: The interview maintains temporal order, distinguishes contemporaneous evidence from later events, and avoids treating an unrelated incident as confirmation of the atrium-design decision. It also differentiates general reputation and anecdotal precedent from system-specific evidence. The paired-scenario counterfactual variable is correctly not enacted in this vocabulary-control condition.

global_revision_constraints: Maintain the zero-target-bias requirement for the vocabulary-control condition.
Do not convert relevant expertise, targeted risk management, sampling logic, or post-event causal separation into bias evidence.
Preserve the four-decision-point structure, chronology, technical vocabulary, occupational setting, and approximately current narrative length.
If future stylistic editing occurs, retain the explicit safeguards that neutralize apparent authority, ambiguity, clustering, base-rate, optimism, and hindsight cues.
